_schema.description: Standards for writing and updating Module READMEs in Forms Portal — documents for code that already exists and is running. Covers Django app READMEs (form_builder, form_respondent, etc.) and forms_toolkit/ module READMEs. These are LIVING DOCUMENTS that must stay in sync with the code they describe.

companion_standards.readme_standards_plan: .specify/memory/standards/readme_standards_plan.json — for Feature Specifications, Implementation Plans, and Architecture Notes

_usage._note_to_agent: READ THIS BLOCK FIRST. It tells you whether this file applies to the README you are about to write or edit.
applies_to: Django app READMEs: <app_name>/README.md — e.g. form_builder/README.md, form_respondent/README.md
Any README documenting code that is ALREADY RUNNING
use_when: Writing a README for a Django app whose views, models, and services are already implemented
Writing a README for a forms_toolkit/ module that is already tested and passing
Updating an existing Module README because the code it documents changed (bug fix, new feature, refactor)
Adding mermaid diagrams to a README for shipped code
do_not_use_when: Writing a Feature Specification or Implementation Plan for UNIMPLEMENTED work — use .specify/memory/standards/readme_standards_plan.json instead
Writing an Architecture Note (ideas/arch_*.md) — use readme_standards_plan.json
Writing a tasks.md file — that is managed by spec-kit /speckit-tasks
_usage.core_distinction_from_plan: A Module README is under a MAINTENANCE CONTRACT: when the code changes, this README must change in the SAME commit. A plan-stage document is a time-bounded design artifact that gets frozen at ship time. If you cannot maintain a Module README in sync with the code, delete the stale content — do not leave lies.
_usage.why_this_file_exists: spec-kit provides templates for spec.md and plan.md but NOT for Module READMEs. This file is the quality rulebook for all shipped-code documentation — it enforces present-tense voice, maintenance contract, mermaid rules, and the Quick Reference Card that makes READMEs agent-navigable.

readme_header.description: Every Module README must have a consistent header block at the top.
required_fields: # <ModuleName> — <Short tagline>   (H1 — document title, one per file)
**Last updated:** YYYY-MM-DD (vN.N)   (update every time the file changes; bump inline version)
**Last git commit:** YYYY-MM-DD        (last commit that touched this module's source code)
rules: The H1 title is the only H1 in the entire file
All major sections use H2 (##); subsections use H3 (###); rarely H4
**Last updated** MUST be updated whenever any section changes
**Last git commit** MUST be filled by running: git log -1 --format='%Y-%m-%d' -- <module_path>/
Date format: YYYY-MM-DD
Include an 'Agent note' callout immediately after the header block citing the applicable standards file: .specify/memory/standards/readme_standards_shipped.json
example: ## Pure-Python validation for all Forms Portal field types
> **Agent note:** This is a Module README documenting shipped code. When editing, follow `.specify/memory/standards/readme_standards_shipped.json`.

index_section.description: Every Module README must have an Index section immediately after the header block.
index_section.position: First section after the opening --- divider
index_section.heading: ## Index
index_section.format: Markdown table with columns: # | Section | Summary
rules: Row 0 is always the Agent Quick Reference Card — label it 'Start here'
Row numbers match the order sections appear in the document
Each row links to the section anchor using markdown link syntax: [Label](#anchor)
Anchor format: GitHub Flavored Markdown (lowercase, spaces to hyphens, remove non-alphanumeric except hyphens)
Summary column: ONE CONCISE LINE — no full paragraphs

quick_reference_card.description: REQUIRED for all Module READMEs. A dense agent speed-reading section that covers 80% of tasks in ~20-50 lines.
quick_reference_card.heading: ## Agent Quick Reference Card
quick_reference_card.position: Immediately after the Index section, before section 1
required_subsections: Opening blockquote — 'Read this first' + link back to Index
### Public API — import statements + function/endpoint table (signature or URL, return type, use case)
### Key Constants — any constants that must never be changed, with inline warning comment
### Consumers — table of files that import from or call this module and what they use
### Hard Rules — numbered list of rules where violation causes bugs (max 5-8 rules)
Closing blockquote — 'Need more detail? Use the Index.' with link
rules: Opening line MUST say: 'Read this first. For 80% of tasks this is all you need.'
Opening line MUST include a link back to the Index: [Index](#index)
Closing line MUST say: 'Need more detail? Use the [Index](#index) to jump directly to the section you need.'
Function table columns: Function | Returns | Use for
Hard Rules must be numbered, bolded rule name, then explanation after em dash
Keep total length under 120 lines — if longer, move detail to a dedicated section and link to it
Never duplicate information that is ONLY needed for deep-dive tasks
Quick Reference Card is for CURRENT SHIPPED API only — NEVER list future or planned APIs here

required_sections.description: Two section lists — one per architecture layer. Use the list matching the module you are documenting. Quick Reference Card and Index are required for both.
required_sections._note: Never omit Overview, Quick Reference Card, Index, or Version History from either layer.

layer_1_forms_toolkit.use_for: forms_toolkit/ pure-Python modules — field validators, schema parsers, export formatters, scoring engines

sections.heading: ## Overview
sections.content: Metadata table: Location, Type, Purpose, Status, Tests, Key dependencies. Plus links to any companion spec/plan docs.

sections.heading: ## Why This Exists
sections.content: What gap this module fills. What the alternative (no module, or a simpler approach) would have looked like and why it was rejected. Past-tense, concise.

sections.heading: ## Current Features
sections.content: Two sub-tables: 'Implemented' (Feature | File | Description) and 'Not in scope' (NOT here | Where it belongs). ONLY list features that are SHIPPED — no 'coming soon'.

sections.heading: ## Architecture / Design
sections.content: Diagrams (ASCII or mermaid — follow mermaid_diagrams rules), sub-sections for module structure, data flow, key invariants. Every diagram label must map to a real function, class, or constant in the code.

sections.heading: ## File Structure
sections.content: Tree view of all files with inline comments explaining each file's role. Must match the actual directory — verify against the filesystem.

sections.heading: ## Quick Start
sections.content: Copy-paste Python examples for the 2-3 most common use cases. No explanation — just working code. Must run with: python -c 'from forms_toolkit...' in a fresh virtualenv.

sections.heading: ## TODO List
sections.content: Minor improvements only — items that take under 2 hours and need no new module or model. Table: # | Task | Reason. Three priority sub-sections: High / Medium / Low. Any larger work belongs in a new Feature Specification via /speckit-specify.

sections.heading: ## Running Tests
sections.content: Bash code block with pytest commands: single file, full module, with -v. Must work when copy-pasted from the project root.

sections.heading: ## Test Configuration Details
sections.content: Fixtures table (Fixture | What it creates). Edge cases covered list. Omit only if module has zero tests.

sections.heading: ## Configuration Reference
sections.content: Dataclass fields table (Field | Type | Default | Notes). Any environment-specific behavior. Include the standalone __main__ test block usage if one exists.

sections.heading: ## Output Format
sections.content: Return value examples for each public function. Show the success case and the error/empty case. For dataclass returns, show the full field structure. This is the most-read section for agent callers.

sections.heading: ## Related Files
sections.content: Table of files that produce or consume this module. Columns: File | Role. Include any known import constraints.

sections.heading: ## Version History
sections.content: Table: Version | Date | Description. Most recent at top. WHAT changed and WHY — never 'updated README'.

layer_2_django_app.use_for: Django app READMEs — portal_core, form_builder, form_respondent, response_viewer, analytics, user_auth, and any future Django app

sections.heading: ## Overview
sections.content: Metadata table: Location, Type, Purpose, Status, Tests, Key dependencies. URLs namespace. Plus links to any companion spec/plan docs.

sections.heading: ## Why This Exists
sections.content: What user-facing or platform need this app serves. What the alternative would have looked like and why this app boundary was chosen. Past-tense, concise.

sections.heading: ## Current Features
sections.content: Two sub-tables: 'Implemented' (Feature | File | Description) and 'Not in scope' (NOT here | Where it belongs). ONLY list features that are SHIPPED — no 'coming soon'.

sections.heading: ## Architecture / Design
sections.content: Diagrams (ASCII or mermaid — follow mermaid_diagrams rules), sub-sections for layers, request flow, HTMX interaction model. Every diagram label must map to a real view, service, model, or URL name.

sections.heading: ## File Structure
sections.content: Tree view of all files with inline comments. Must match the actual directory — verify against the filesystem.

sections.heading: ## Quick Start
sections.content: Setup steps: URL include, settings entry, migration command. Copy-paste ready. Must result in the app being accessible when followed.

sections.heading: ## TODO List
sections.content: Minor improvements only — items that take under 2 hours and need no new model, service, or architectural change. Table: # | Task | Reason. Three priority sub-sections: High / Medium / Low. Any larger work belongs in a new Feature Specification via /speckit-specify.

sections.heading: ## Running Tests
sections.content: Bash code block with pytest-django commands: single file, full app, with -v. Must work when copy-pasted from the project root.

sections.heading: ## Test Configuration Details
sections.content: Fixtures table (Fixture | What it creates). Edge cases covered list. Omit only if app has zero tests.

sections.heading: ## HTMX Endpoints
sections.content: Table of all HTMX-specific views: URL name | Method | hx-target | Response partial | Triggered by. This replaces 'Output Format' for Django apps — agents need to know what each view returns, not Python return values.

sections.heading: ## Configuration Reference
sections.content: settings.py entries required by this app. URL namespace and include pattern. Any environment variables. Admin URL if the app registers admin pages.

sections.heading: ## Related Files
sections.content: Table of files that this app imports from or that import from this app. Columns: File | Role.

sections.heading: ## Version History
sections.content: Table: Version | Date | Description. Most recent at top. WHAT changed and WHY — never 'updated README'.

version_history_rules.description: Rules for maintaining the Version History section in Module READMEs.
rules: Add a new row at the TOP of the table for every significant update
Version format: major.minor (e.g. 1.0, 1.1, 2.0)
Increment MINOR for: README corrections, new sections, diagram additions, docstring-level fixes
Increment MAJOR for: new public functions, new models, architectural changes, new sections that change the mental model of the module
Date format: YYYY-MM-DD
Description must state WHAT changed and WHY — NOT 'updated README'
Also update **Last updated:** in the header to match the latest version date
If the change added a mermaid diagram, the description MUST note which code symbols the diagram was verified against
version_history_rules.example_row: | 1.2 | 2026-05-20 | Added mermaid stateDiagram to Architecture section showing form lifecycle (Draft → Published → Archived → Deleted). Every label verified against FormStatus choices in forms_toolkit/schema.py. |

mermaid_diagrams.description: Rules for adding mermaid diagrams to Module READMEs. GitHub renders mermaid natively. A good mermaid saves 30+ seconds of reading; a bad one silently lies when the code drifts. Default stance: NO DIAGRAM until a diagram earns its place.
rules: 1. JUSTIFY EACH DIAGRAM — Would this save the reader 30+ seconds of text reading? Does it make a decision flow instantly obvious? If no, use a table or prose instead. Mermaid is not decoration.
2. NEVER DUPLICATE TABLES — If a markdown table already shows the same information, do NOT also add a mermaid. One source of truth per fact.
3. CO-LOCATE WITH THE TEXT — Place each diagram immediately next to the prose it illustrates so an edit to one forces the writer to look at the other. Diagrams separated from their text rot silently.
4. STALENESS IS WORSE THAN ABSENCE — A mermaid that contradicts the current code is worse than no mermaid, because readers trust visuals more than prose. If you cannot keep it in sync, delete it.
5. MAX ONE DIAGRAM PER CONCEPT — If a section needs more than one mermaid to explain a single idea, the idea is too big for a diagram and belongs in prose + a table.

6. USE THE RIGHT DIAGRAM TYPE — flowchart for data/control flow, stateDiagram-v2 for lifecycle states, sequenceDiagram for time-ordered HTMX interactions, classDiagram rarely (usually a table is better).

7. LABEL DENSITY — Labels must be specific enough to understand the diagram WITHOUT the surrounding prose. 'Process' is useless. 'forms_toolkit.validator.validate_field() → FieldError | None' is good.
8. COLOR DELIBERATELY — classDef with a semantic palette (one color per concept: storage=blue, validation=green, decision=amber, error=red). Never decorative colors.

9. TEST IN THE RENDERER — Before committing, verify the diagram renders in GitHub's markdown preview. Parse errors usually mean HTML entities in labels — put labels in quotes and use
for newlines.
10. MAX ~8 DIAGRAMS PER MODULE README — more than that signals the README is trying to document too much at once.
good_candidates: Form lifecycle states (Draft → Published → Archived) — stateDiagram-v2
Field branching logic (condition check → show/hide) — flowchart TD
HTMX request/response cycle for form submission — sequenceDiagram
Two-layer architecture (forms_toolkit → service → view) — flowchart LR
RBAC role resolution (Owner vs Collaborator element states) — flowchart TD
Field UUID versioning model (response storage across form edits) — flowchart LR
bad_candidates: Section tables of contents (the Index already handles this)
Anything already perfectly captured by a markdown table
Pure enumerations with no relationships (use a bullet list)
Decorative 'overview' diagrams with 4 boxes and no meaningful edges
Diagrams that repeat another diagram with trivial visual tweaks
Diagrams where label density is so high they are unreadable on mobile
maintenance_contract: When you edit code that a mermaid diagram describes, you MUST update the diagram in the same commit. No exceptions.
When reviewing a PR, treat stale mermaid labels the same as stale docstrings — a review blocker.
If you cannot figure out how to update a diagram, the diagram was too ambitious — delete it and replace with prose + a table.
Every mermaid diagram must have at least one label that names a real function, class, field, or constant. Zero real identifiers = decorative = delete it.

When adding a new mermaid, grep the code for every function/class name that will appear as a label and confirm it exists. Do NOT document code that does not exist yet — that belongs in a plan-stage document.

rules: H1 (#): Document title only — exactly ONE per file
H2 (##): Major sections (Index, Quick Reference Card, Overview, Why This Exists, etc.)
H3 (###): Subsections within a major section
H4 (####): Only if a subsection itself needs sub-grouping — use sparingly
Never skip levels (do not jump from H1 to H3)

anchor_generation.description: How GitHub Flavored Markdown generates anchor IDs from headings — used for Index links.
algorithm: 1. Take the heading text (exclude the # prefix)
3. Remove all characters that are not letters, digits, spaces, or hyphens
5. Leading/trailing hyphens from stripped characters are kept
anchor_generation.duplicate_anchor_warning: If two headings produce the same anchor, GitHub appends -1, -2, etc. Avoid duplicate heading text across the file.

agent_update_workflow.description: Step-by-step process an agent MUST follow when updating an existing Module README.
steps: 1. Read the FULL README first — do not skim
2. Identify what CODE changed (new function? bug fix? refactor? new model? new HTMX endpoint?)
3. Update the relevant section(s) with accurate information — every label, function name, and field name must match the current code
4. If a mermaid diagram describes the changed code, UPDATE THE DIAGRAM IN THE SAME EDIT (maintenance contract)
5. Update the Quick Reference Card if the public API, consumers, hard rules, or HTMX endpoints changed
6. Update the Index if any section was added, removed, or renamed
7. Add a new row to Version History describing all changes made (WHAT and WHY, never 'updated README')
8. Update **Last updated:** in the header to today's date and bump inline version
9. Do NOT change sections that are unrelated to the update
10. If any change added or modified a mermaid diagram, verify it renders in GitHub's markdown preview before committing
when_to_update_quick_reference_card: New public function or HTMX endpoint added or removed
Service layer result dataclass fields changed

claude_md_ledger.description: How to maintain the CLAUDE.md 'Implemented' ledger — the per-feature as-built record loaded into agent context EVERY session. Keep it scannable; the archive is the durable full record.
rules: One '**Implemented**: `###-feature`' entry per shipped feature, newest first.

Keep only the newest ~7 features FULL inline. When a new feature ships, DEMOTE the oldest full entry to a 3-line summary (what it did · key lesson/DR · spec + archive pointer) and MOVE its full text under a '## NNN-name' anchor in .specify/ledger_archive.md.

Older features live as a 3-line summary or a one-line pointer to .specify/ledger_archive.md#NNN-name. Never DELETE an entry — archive it. Every shipped feature stays reachable (full inline / 3-line summary / pointer).

Reusable PATTERNS + cross-cutting rules do NOT belong in the ledger — they live in decision records + the CLAUDE.md 'durable fact' sections (which stay loaded). The ledger is per-feature as-built only.
Rationale: a ~600-word single-line entry x N features bloats the always-loaded context. On 2026-07-18 an overdue archive pass cut CLAUDE.md 313 KB -> 124 KB doing exactly this.

writing_style.description: Writing style rules for Module READMEs.
rules: Use PRESENT TENSE and indicative mood — 'the service returns X', 'the view renders Y'. No 'we will', 'planned', 'coming soon' — that language belongs in Feature Specifications
Use tables over bullet lists for structured data (functions, files, features, endpoints)
Use bullet lists for sequential steps or non-tabular lists
Use blockquotes (>) for critical agent-facing instructions or warnings
Bold (**text**) only for: rule names in Hard Rules, column headers, critical warnings
Code blocks for all import statements, function signatures, URL patterns, and config snippets
Inline code (`text`) for: function names, file paths, constant names, model field names, URL names
ASCII diagrams for simple flows; mermaid for complex multi-branch flows (follow mermaid_diagrams rules)
Avoid filler phrases like 'This section describes...' — go straight to the content
Section summaries in the Index must be ONE concise line
Never document what is planned — only what is SHIPPED. Planned work belongs in a Feature Specification under .specify/specs/

cross_reference_interlinking.description: Rules for adding clickable links between sections within the same README. Makes the document navigable without scrolling.
rules: Every time a section mentions another section by name, make it a clickable link: [Section Name](#anchor)
Use the same anchor format as the Index
Each section should have a 1-2 line intro linking to prerequisite and related sections BEFORE its content starts
The Quick Reference Card Hard Rules should each link to the section with full detail
Do NOT over-link — only link when the reference is meaningful

minimum_links.medium_readme: 500-1500 lines: Index + 5-10 cross-references in key sections
minimum_links.large_readme: over 1500 lines: Index + 15+ cross-references + section intros

live_document_contract.description: Module READMEs are LIVING DOCUMENTS under a maintenance contract. This is the single most important difference from plan-stage documents.
rules: When the code changes, this README MUST change in the SAME commit. No 'I will update the README later'.
When reviewing a PR that touches code described by a section or diagram here, the review MUST check that the corresponding README content is still accurate. Stale doc = review blocker.

If you cannot keep a section accurate (the code is too volatile or the mechanism too subtle), DELETE the section rather than leave it stale. An accurate 500-line README beats a drifting 2000-line README.
Every fact in this README should be traceable to a specific file or symbol in the code. If you find an assertion you cannot trace, investigate — it is either wrong, outdated, or speculative.
